© Vladimir Grigorev
By Charlotte Goldstone
17 November 2026
Warehouse operators are ramping up investment in artificial intelligence and automation, despite continuing difficulties proving the financial benefits, according to new research published today.
A study by MIT’s Intelligent Logistics Systems Lab and warehouse technology provider Mecalux found that 90% of companies expect to increase spending on generative and agentic AI over the next two to three years.
The MIT–Mecalux research, involving 1,967 supply chain and warehousing professionals across 21 countries, found 83% had already reported accelerating AI adoption in the past year.
However, although 87% of generative AI applications and 81% of agentic AI applications reportedly delivered at least moderate operational improvements, only 39% and 36%, respectively, achieved significant gains that could be supported by documented figures.
Around three in ten formal return-on-investment assessments were inconclusive or below expectations, according to the research.
The study also found that 40% of organisations had abandoned at least one AI initiative over the past two years – integration difficulties, poor data quality, and disappointing returns among the principal reasons.
The findings come as major logistics operators GXO and Ceva unveiled ambitious plans to expand the use of robotics and AI in their warehouse operations.
Ceva Logistics today announced a five-year collaboration with the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) to establish the Intelligent Logistics & Autonomous Systems Lab, supported by the Singapore Economic Development Board and National Robotics Programme.
It will focus on automating labour-intensive, high-mix, low-volume value-added services (VAS), including kitting, labelling, and packing, using robotics, AI vision systems, and connected automation.
Ceva said VAS accounted for approximately half the warehouse floor hours at its automated Blue Hub facility in Singapore, where solutions developed through the lab are expected to be deployed within one to two years.
Guy Meredith, Ceva’s contract logistics VP, APAC, said: “Our ambition is to build on validated solutions for new applications across customer sectors and our Asia Pacific network, using lessons from each deployment to shape further innovation.”
Meanwhile, during GXO Logistics’ Investor Day yesterday, the company outlined automation-led growth targets to 2030 of annual organic revenue growth exceeding 7%, and an adjusted EBITA margin above 6.5%.
According to the presentation, approximately 40% of GXO’s operations are already automated, compared with its estimate of an industry average of 15% to 20%.
The company said it expected automation, warehouse AI, and adaptive technology to generate an additional $50m–$70m in annual EBITA run-rate savings over the four-year plan.
GXO also identified Asia-Pacific, Mexico, and Central and Eastern Europe as expansion opportunities, although its presentation did not specify funded warehouse projects across those markets.
Last week, GXO announced a letter of intent with robotics developer Apptronik to expand trials of Apollo humanoid robots, potentially deploying up to 1,000 units over four years. The proposal remains conditional on further development and successful trials, rather than representing a confirmed purchase commitment.
The MIT–Mecalux study found that 57% of respondents expected AI to execute more than 25% of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028.
Inevitably this highlighted human workforce implications, with 56% reporting that AI had shifted employees towards higher-value tasks, while 11% reported headcount reductions.
